title: Permutations
statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations in any order.
realWorld: Exhaustive search over orderings: brute-forcing a small travelling-salesman instance, testing every execution interleaving in a concurrency test, or trying join orders in a query planner.

bruteForce.idea: Every ordering of n items has a unique rank in [0, n!) once you fix an encoding: read rank in the factorial number system to get one digit per position, and let that digit choose (and remove) an element from the list of what is still unplaced. Looping rank from 0 to n!-1 and decoding each one enumerates every permutation without ever choosing and un-choosing recursively.
code: int index = (int) (r / f);      // this digit of the factorial-base encoding of rank
for (int i = 2; i <= k; i++) f *= i;

complexity.space: O(n) per candidate, plus the n! results

bruteForce.whySlow: The decode is done from scratch for every one of the n! ranks: a fresh remaining-list is rebuilt and walked position by position, and a factorial is recomputed at each step, none of which is reused between one rank and the next. It also does strictly more bookkeeping per permutation than backtracking's choose/un-choose — an ArrayList.remove(index) is O(n) on its own, so building all n! permutations this way costs O(n^2 * n!) against backtracking's O(n * n!). The insight backtracking uses instead is that consecutive permutations it visits share almost their entire prefix, so the placed elements never need to be rebuilt, only the one at the frontier — information this rank-by-rank decoding throws away and recomputes every time.

patternIdentification: 'All orderings' means order matters and every unused element is a candidate at every position — backtracking with a used[] marker rather than a start index.

optimized.idea: Build the permutation position by position. At each position try every element not already placed; mark it used, recurse, then unmark.
code: backtrack(nums, new ArrayList<>(), new boolean[nums.length], result);
private static void backtrack(int[] nums, List<Integer> current, boolean[] used,

complexity.space: O(n) recursion depth, excluding the output

commonMistakes: Using a start index (as in subsets) instead of used[] — that generates combinations, not permutations.
Resetting used[i] but forgetting to remove the element from current, or the reverse. Undo both.
Storing the live list rather than a copy.
With duplicate values, producing repeated permutations; sort first and skip nums[i] == nums[i-1] when used[i-1] is false.
